conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists on your care team. You're here today for your first maintenance dose of high-dose methotrexate after completing reinduction therapy for your CNS lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Doctor. Yes, I’ve been feeling really well since my last cycle. No dizziness or weakness at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent to hear. The MRI showed good response—your right occipital lesion has resolved, which is a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean the treatment is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. It shows the reinduction therapy was effective, and now we’re moving into maintenance to help prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So today is just one infusion, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get the methotrexate infusion this afternoon at 4 p.m. It usually takes a few hours. We’ll also give you IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin? When does that start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Leucovorin rescue starts exactly 24 hours after the methotrexate infusion ends. We’ll continue it until your methotrexate levels drop to a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I remember from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your sodium bicarbonate through the IV to keep your urine alkaline. This helps flush out the methotrexate safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on oral bicarbonate at home too. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your usual dose by mouth as well. It’s important to keep your urine pH above 7.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any blood tests today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll check your electrolytes, kidney and liver function, and a complete blood count. We’ll monitor your potassium closely because the bicarbonate can lower it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, right. I had low potassium last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your infusion started about 5 minutes ago. It’ll run for approximately 4 hours. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m fine so far. Just a little anxious, but that’s normal for me in hospitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’re monitoring you closely. Let us know if you feel nauseous, dizzy, or have any pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your infusion just finished. Great job—you tolerated it very well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. When do the side effects usually start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people don’t feel much during the infusion. Some get mild nausea or fatigue in the next day or two. We’ve given you ondansetron just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your potassium is a bit low, at 3.3. We’re giving you some IV potassium to bring it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the bicarbonate again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It shifts potassium into cells, so we have to replace it. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver tests? Last time they went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your AST and ALT are elevated—119 and 142—but that’s expected with methotrexate. They should come down in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a known side effect and we monitor it closely. Nothing concerning at this level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s your stomach? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little queasy this morning, but the ondansetron helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep taking it as needed. Also, are your bowels moving okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took the senna and magnesium citrate like usual. No constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Staying regular helps avoid discomfort during treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level came back at 0.05, which is excellent. That means it’s clearing well from your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that means I’m safe to stop the leucovorin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give one more dose today and then stop. Your kidneys are handling everything well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And my headache? It’s back a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take your usual acetaminophen-caffeine-butalbital for it. Headaches can happen around this time, but yours isn’t severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll take one now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. Thompson. You’re doing so well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with your usual meds: docusate, senna, magnesium citrate, omeprazole, aspirin, and sodium bicarbonate. Also ondansetron for nausea if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was on ranitidine during the infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we switched to ranitidine to avoid any interaction with the methotrexate. Now you can go back to omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And aspirin? I stopped it last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We hold aspirin during treatment due to bleeding risk with low platelets, but your count is stable, so you can restart it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your oncologist next week for rituximab. Then return here in one month for your next methotrexate dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll mark it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Final check before discharge. You’re alert, your neuro exam is normal, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Walked around the unit this morning—no dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your gait is steady, strength is full, and you’re independent. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Keep up the good work—staying active and managing your symptoms is key. Call if you have fever, severe nausea, or new neurological symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see the oncologist next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final visit. Your discharge is set for 10:15 a.m. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think we covered everything. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. You did great this admission—tolerated the chemo well, no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for making it smooth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is here to support you. See you next month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, stay hydrated, and keep taking your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.
